title: Yichud: Alone Together
hookLine: the couple spends a few minutes alone right after the ceremony
carry: a marriage begins with time set apart
tomorrow: These and These: When Movements Differ

lines: A SMALL ROOM DOWN THE HALL.
cards: A small side room, down the hall from the party. A table, two chairs, a little food. The door closes, and a couple of friends stand outside it so nobody knocks.

Inside are two people married a few minutes ago, alone together for the first time all day. Down the hall the band is tuning up, the photographer is checking the light, the guests are finding their tables.
For a short while, nobody can reach the two of them. The room has a name, and so do these minutes.

teach.b: Yichud means being alone together, and it belongs to the wedding; it isn't a break from it. Some authorities count these minutes alone, as a married couple, as part of the wedding itself.
The friends at the door serve as witnesses that the two were alone together. Then there's the meal. In some communities the bride and groom fast on their wedding day until the ceremony.

teach.h: THE FIRST MEAL, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: The food in that room is where they break the fast side by side, the first meal of their marriage, with no one else at the table. Behind it is a law in Deuteronomy.
A new husband isn't sent out to war or loaded with public duties.

teach.h: FREE AT HOME, THE TORAH SAYS.
teach.b: In the King James words, "he shall be free at home one year, and shall cheer up his wife which he hath taken." The Torah treats the start of a marriage as something the world should leave alone for a while.
Yichud is that idea in miniature: a few minutes the whole day agrees not to touch.
Before the speeches and photos, before anyone else takes a piece of the day, there's a moment that belongs only to the two of them.

Whatever they say in there, or don't, is theirs. Then the door opens, and they walk out to the music. A shared life needs a little protected quiet at its start, and the people who love them keep watch at the door.

how: Right after a traditional Jewish wedding ceremony, the couple spends a few minutes alone in a private room (yichud), often breaking a wedding-day fast together, while friends stand by the door as witnesses.

o: a private prayer the groom says before the vows

games.q: the ceremony just ended, and you want a photo with the couple. they're heading down the hall to a small room. what do you do?
o: ask the friends at the door to let you in.
games.why: yichud gives the couple their first moment alone; friends stand at the door so nobody knocks.

practice: Bring to mind someone who rarely gets a moment to themselves, a parent of small children, a caregiver, a friend always on call, and picture one small way you could stand at their door: a task taken off their hands, the noise kept down.
If you're the one who never gets quiet, let these minutes be yours, and let nobody knock.

wordCard.voice: Yichud: alone together, right after the ceremony. And a week closes: a match, conditions, the canopy, the ketubah read, seven blessings, the glass, and the first moment. Today's word.
